sub: Named after an-nāziʿāt, “those who pull out”, its opening word
theme: The Resurrection is certain and easy for Allah. Firʿawn’s end is a warning, the sky and earth are the proof, and each person’s home depends on whether he feared his Lord or followed his desires.
story: Revealed in Makkah in the earliest period, reportedly right after An-Nabaʾ, and on the same theme: the Resurrection, the Hereafter, and what happens to those who deny the Messenger.

The deniers of Makkah laughed at the idea of rotten bones living again, and joked that such a return would be a loss. They also kept asking the Prophet ﷺ, mockingly, when the Hour would come. Their stubbornness hurt him.
The surah answers them: it takes one shout; Firʿawn’s end shows where denial leads; the sky is harder to make than you; and the Hour’s time is with Allah alone. The Prophet ﷺ is only a warner.

sections.title: Oaths by the angels, then one blast
sections.meaning: Allah swears by the angels who pull out souls, harshly or gently, glide, race ahead and carry out His commands. The first blast shakes everything, the second follows, and hearts tremble. The deniers ask how rotten bones could live again. It takes one shout, and they are all standing on the earth.
points: By angels who pull souls out harshly, and gently
Who glide, race ahead, and carry out commands
Blast after blast; hearts tremble, eyes lowered
“Brought back, after rotten bones? A losing return!”
Just one shout, and they are on the open earth
sections.matters: It answers the deniers’ biggest doubt. The angels who take souls at death show Allah’s control over life, and bringing everyone back takes no effort: a single shout. The oath’s answer is left unsaid, but the scene makes it plain: you will be raised.
sections.story: No specific incident. It answers Makkah’s deniers, who mocked the idea of rotten bones coming back to life.
explained: The oaths are by angels. An-nāziʿāt pull out the souls of disbelievers with force; an-nāshiṭāt draw out the souls of believers gently, like untying a knot. They glide through the air, race to carry out Allah’s command, and arrange the affairs He puts in their charge.

Ar-rājifah, the first blast, shakes everything; ar-rādifah, the second, follows. Hearts pound and eyes are lowered. Yet in this world the deniers say: “Us, brought back after we are hollow bones? That would be a losing return!” The reply: it is only one zajrah, one shout, and suddenly all are standing on the earth’s surface.
teaches: Death is in the hands of angels acting on Allah’s command.
Bringing everyone back takes Allah just one shout.
Mocking the Hereafter doesn’t cancel it.
Prepare now for the Day hearts will tremble.
sections.hook: Five oaths, all plurals ending in -āt: nāziʿāt, nāshiṭāt, sābiḥāt, sābiqāt, mudabbirāt. The first three start with wa, the last two with fa. It begins on page 583, where An-Nabaʾ ends.

sections.title: The story of Mūsā and Firʿawn
sections.meaning: Allah called Mūsā in the sacred valley of Ṭuwā and sent him to the arrogant Firʿawn with a gentle offer: purify yourself and know your Lord. Mūsā showed the great sign. Firʿawn denied it, gathered his people and declared, “I am your lord, most high.” Allah seized him, a lesson for whoever fears.
points: Has Mūsā’s story reached you? Called in the valley of Ṭuwā
Go to Firʿawn: will you purify yourself and fear your Lord?
The great sign; he denied, disobeyed and turned away
He gathered them: “I am your lord, most high”
Seized in this world and the next: a lesson
sections.matters: It shows the deniers of Makkah where arrogance ends: the most powerful ruler rejected his messenger and was destroyed. It also comforts the Prophet ﷺ: earlier prophets faced the same stubbornness and stayed patient.
sections.story: The Prophet ﷺ was hurt by the stubbornness of those who denied the Resurrection. This story was told to console him, and to warn them that Firʿawn met his end for rejecting a messenger.
explained: Allah called Mūsā in the sacred valley of Ṭuwā and sent him to Firʿawn, who had grown arrogant and crossed every limit. The message was gentle: “Would you like to purify yourself? I will guide you to your Lord, so you fear Him.” Then Mūsā showed him the greatest sign, the staff and the shining hand.

Firʿawn knew it was true, yet he denied it and disobeyed. He turned away, working against the truth, gathered his people and proclaimed: “I am your lord, the most high.” So Allah seized him: drowned in this world, punished in the next. In that is a lesson for anyone who fears Allah.
teaches: Knowing the truth isn’t enough without submitting to it.
Arrogance against Allah ends in ruin, here and hereafter.
Only a heart that fears Allah learns from lessons.
sections.hook: It opens with a question, hal atāka (15), and closes with ʿibrah, a lesson (26). Firʿawn’s actions come in pairs: kadhdhaba wa-ʿaṣā (21), ḥashara fa-nādā (23). Page 584 starts at ayah 17.

sections.title: Harder to create: you or the sky?
sections.meaning: Are you harder to create, or the sky? Allah built it, raised it high and made it flawless, darkened its night and brought out its daylight. Then He spread out the earth, brought out its water and pasture, and set the mountains firm: provision for you and your livestock.
points: Are you harder to create, or the sky He built?
Raised high and even; dark night, bright morning
The earth spread out: its water and its pasture
Mountains set firm: provision for you and your livestock
sections.matters: It answers “rotten bones” with plain logic: making you again is small next to making the sky. And a world arranged this carefully for your needs was made with purpose, so its people will be raised and held to account.
sections.story: No specific incident. It returns to the deniers of the Resurrection with a proof they can see.
explained: Which is harder to make: you, or the vast sky above you? Clearly the sky. Allah built it, raised its height and made it flawless, with no cracks. He made its night dark and brought out its ḍuḥā, the brightness of its day. If He did that, bringing you back is easy.

After that He spread out the earth. The earth itself was made before the sky, but spread out after it, when He brought out its springs, its pasture and its hidden benefits. He fixed the mountains so the earth stays steady. All of it is matāʿ, provision for you and your livestock.
teaches: If Allah made the sky, remaking you is easy.
Water, pasture and mountains were set up for your benefit.
A world made with such care was not made for nothing.
sections.hook: Six ayat in a row rhyme on -āhā (27–32): bināhā, sawwāhā, ḍuḥāhā, daḥāhā, marʿāhā, arsāhā. Sky comes first (27–29), then earth (30–33). Akhraja is used twice (29, 31).

sections.title: The Great Catastrophe: two final homes
sections.meaning: When the Great Catastrophe comes, every person remembers what he strove for, and Hell is brought out for all to see. Whoever transgressed and preferred this world: Hell is his home. Whoever feared standing before his Lord and held himself back from desire: Paradise is his home.
points: The Great Catastrophe: man remembers; Hell brought into view
Transgressed and preferred this world → Hell
Feared his Lord, restrained desire → Paradise
sections.matters: This is the dividing line. It gives the two traits that lead to each home, so a person can check himself now: am I chasing this world and my desires, or holding back because I will stand before Allah?
sections.story: Reportedly revealed about a disbelieving brother of Muṣʿab ibn ʿUmayr (37–39) and Muṣʿab himself (40–41). Other reports name Abū Jahl, an-Naḍr and his son, or Abū Bakr. Either way, the ayat describe every person.
explained: Aṭ-ṭāmmah al-kubrā, the Great Catastrophe, is the Day of Judgement, named so because it overwhelms every other disaster. Each person then remembers all he did, good and bad, when remembering can no longer help. Hell is uncovered and brought out in plain view for everyone to see.

Then there are two kinds of people. One ṭaghā, went past the limits, and preferred this life, spending his effort and time on its pleasures and forgetting the Hereafter: Hell is his home. The other feared standing before his Lord and stopped his soul from its desires: Paradise is his home.
teaches: Everything you do, you will remember that Day.
Preferring this world over the Hereafter leads to Hell.
Fear of standing before Allah is what holds desire back.
Paradise is for whoever says no to his own desires.
sections.hook: Two mirror pairs: fa-ammā man (37) and wa-ammā man (40). Each ends with the same words, hiya al-maʾwā (39, 41); only al-jaḥīm and al-jannah differ.

sections.title: They ask: when is the Hour?
sections.meaning: They keep asking when the Hour will come. Telling its time is not the Prophet’s ﷺ task; its knowledge ends with Allah. He is only a warner for those who fear it. When they see it, their whole stay will feel like one evening or its morning.
points: They ask you about the Hour: when will it arrive?
Not yours to tell; its end is with your Lord
You only warn those who fear it
Life will feel like an afternoon or a morning
sections.matters: It closes the surah by turning the question around. The date doesn’t matter; being ready does. The Prophet ﷺ is sent to warn, not to announce a date, and life will feel short once that Day arrives.
sections.story: Makkah’s idolaters kept asking the Prophet ﷺ, mockingly, when the Hour would be, and these ayat replied. Reportedly he was pressed about it so often that he asked about it himself, until ayat 43–44 came.
explained: Ayyāna mursāhā: when will it arrive? They asked to mock, not to prepare. The reply: fīma anta min dhikrāhā, telling its time is not your role. Its knowledge ends with your Lord; no angel or prophet was given it. Knowing it would benefit no one, so Allah kept it hidden.

The Prophet ﷺ is a mundhir, a warner, and the warning helps only those who fear that Day. When the deniers see it, their life in the world, or their time in the graves, will feel like ʿashiyyah, one afternoon, or its ḍuḥā, the morning of that day.
teaches: Prepare for the Hour instead of asking when.
Only Allah knows when the Hour will come.
A warning helps only a heart that fears.
This life is short; don’t trade forever for an afternoon.
sections.hook: The -āhā rhyme returns: mursāhā, dhikrāhā, muntahāhā, yakhshāhā, ḍuḥāhā. The last word, ḍuḥāhā (46), already appeared in ayah 29. The section opens with yasʾalūnaka.

groups.text: By the angels who take souls, harshly and gently, who glide, race ahead and carry out Allah’s commands.
The first blast shakes everything, the second follows. Hearts tremble and eyes are lowered.
The deniers say: “Brought back, after we are rotten bones? That would be a losing return!”
It is just one shout, and they are standing on the earth’s surface.
Allah called Mūsā at Ṭuwā: go to the arrogant Firʿawn and invite him to purify himself and fear his Lord.
Mūsā showed the greatest sign; Firʿawn denied, disobeyed and turned away, working against the truth.
He gathered his people and proclaimed: “I am your lord, the most high.”
Allah seized him in this world and the next. A lesson for whoever fears.
Are you harder to create, or the sky? Allah raised it, made it even, darkened its night, lit its day.
He spread the earth, brought out its water and pasture, fixed the mountains: provision for you and your animals.
When the Great Catastrophe comes, man remembers his deeds and Hell is shown to all.
Whoever transgressed and preferred this world, Hell is his home.
Whoever feared standing before his Lord and restrained his desires, Paradise is his home.
They ask when the Hour will come. That is not for you to tell; its knowledge is with your Lord.
You only warn those who fear it. When it comes, life will feel like a single afternoon or morning.

1.explain: Wan-nāziʿāti gharqā: by the angels who pull out souls with great force. Most take it as the souls of disbelievers, dragged out harshly, a pain those around may not see.

2.explain: Wan-nāshiṭāti nashṭā: by the angels who draw out souls gently, like untying a knot. Most take this as the souls of believers, released with ease.

3.explain: Was-sābiḥāti sabḥā: by the angels who glide swiftly through the air like swimmers, going up and down, carrying souls to the sky or bringing Allah’s command.

4.explain: Fas-sābiqāti sabqā: by the angels who race ahead to carry out Allah’s command, taking souls without delay to their good or bad abode.

5.explain: Fal-mudabbirāti amrā: by the angels who arrange the affairs Allah entrusts to them: rain, plants, winds and more. The oath’s answer is left unstated: you will surely be raised.

6.explain: Yawma tarjufu ar-rājifah: the Day the first blast of the Horn shakes everything, and all living things die.

7.explain: Tatbaʿuhā ar-rādifah: the second blast follows it. The first brings death to everything; the second brings everything back to life.

8.explain: Wājifah: hearts that Day pound with fear and alarm at what they see and hear.

9.explain: Abṣāruhā khāshiʿah: their eyes lowered, humbled and disgraced by the terror they see.

10.explain: In this world the deniers say: “Will we really be returned fil-ḥāfirah?” That is, back to our first state, alive again (or, in another view, up from our graves).

11.explain: “…even after we are ʿiẓāman nakhirah, rotten, crumbling bones?” Also read nākhirah: hollow bones the wind whistles through. They thought it impossible.

12.explain: Karratun khāsirah: “then that would be a losing return!” They said it mockingly: if we are brought back, we will be the losers.

13.explain: The reply: it is only zajratun wāḥidah, a single shout, the last blast of the Horn. It is no effort for Allah.

14.explain: Fa-idhā hum bis-sāhirah: and suddenly they are on the open surface of the earth, alive after lying dead inside it, all standing and looking.

15.explain: Hal atāka: has the story of Mūsā reached you? The question, put to the Prophet ﷺ, draws attention to a great and true story.

16.explain: His Lord called him in al-wād al-muqaddas, the purified valley, named Ṭuwā. There Allah spoke to him and chose him as a messenger.

17.explain: “Go to Firʿawn; he has ṭaghā, transgressed”: grown arrogant and rebellious, crossing every limit in disbelief.

18.explain: “Say to him: would you like to tazakkā, purify yourself” from shirk and disobedience, by accepting faith? A gentle, inviting way to speak.

19.explain: “…and let me guide you to your Lord, so you fear Him”: so a hard heart becomes humble and obedient.

20.explain: Mūsā showed him al-āyah al-kubrā, the greatest sign: the staff that became a serpent, or his hand shining white, or both.

21.explain: Firʿawn denied it and disobeyed. He knew the truth, but his heart refused to submit to it.

22.explain: Then he turned his back on faith, yasʿā: working hard against the truth and spreading corruption.

23.explain: Fa-ḥashara fa-nādā: he gathered his people, soldiers and magicians, and called out to them.

24.explain: Anā rabbukum al-aʿlā: “I am your lord, the most high”, meaning no lord above me. His people gave in and went along with it.

25.explain: Nakāl: an exemplary punishment. Either drowning in this world and the Fire in the next, or punishment for his last word (24) and his first: “I know no god for you but me.”

26.explain: ʿIbrah: a lesson. Only those who fear Allah take it; a heart with no fear of Him would not believe even if every sign came.

27.explain: Aʾantum ashaddu khalqan: are you, O deniers, harder to create, or the sky? The sky, clearly. Allah built it, so recreating you is easy.

28.explain: Rafaʿa samkahā: He raised its height. Fa-sawwāhā: and made it even and flawless, with no cracks or faults.

29.explain: Aghṭasha laylahā: He made its night dark. Akhraja ḍuḥāhā: He brought out its daylight, the light of its sun.

30.explain: Daḥāhā: He spread it out. The earth was created before the sky, but spread out after it, with its benefits placed within it.

31.explain: He brought out its water, making springs gush, and its marʿā, pasture: grass and trees for animals, and the food and fruits people eat.

32.explain: Arsāhā: He fixed the mountains firmly in place, so the earth stays steady for those living on it.

33.explain: Matāʿan: all this is provision for you and your anʿām, livestock such as camels, cattle and sheep, for as long as this life lasts.

34.explain: Aṭ-ṭāmmah al-kubrā: the greatest, overwhelming catastrophe, the Day of Judgement (or the second blast), which rises above every other disaster.

35.explain: That Day man remembers everything he strove for, good and bad. Every tie from this world is cut except his deeds.

36.explain: Burrizat al-jaḥīm: Hell is uncovered and brought into full view for everyone who can see.

37.explain: Man ṭaghā: whoever crossed the limit, rebelling and daring to commit major sins.
37.why: Reportedly about a brother of Muṣʿab ibn ʿUmayr, captured at Badr, whom Muṣʿab disowned. Other reports name Abū Jahl, or an-Naḍr and his son al-Ḥārith. It applies to anyone who prefers this world.

38.explain: Āthara al-ḥayāt ad-dunyā: and preferred this worldly life, spending his effort and time on its pleasures and forgetting the Hereafter.

39.explain: Al-jaḥīm is his maʾwā: Hell will be his home, the place he settles.

40.explain: Khāfa maqāma rabbih: he feared the moment he will stand before his Lord to be judged. So he held his nafs back from hawā, desires that pull away from obedience.
40.why: Reportedly about Muṣʿab ibn ʿUmayr, killed by arrows at Uḥud. Or about Abū Bakr, who vomited food he learned came from fortune-telling. Or anyone who could sin in private but stops, fearing Allah.

41.explain: Al-jannah is his maʾwā: Paradise, full of every good and joy, will be his home.

42.explain: Ayyāna mursāhā: when will it arrive and take place? They kept asking this, not to prepare but to mock.
42.why: Makkah’s idolaters asked the Prophet ﷺ, mockingly, when the Hour would come. This ayah was revealed in reply.

43.explain: Fīma anta min dhikrāhā: what have you to do with telling its time? You have no knowledge of it. It may also rebuke the idolaters for asking him.
43.why: Reportedly the Prophet ﷺ was asked about the Hour so often that he asked about it himself, until this ayah and the next came.

44.explain: Ilā rabbika muntahāhā: knowledge of it ends with your Lord. No one else knows it, and there is no benefit for people in knowing it.

45.explain: Innamā anta mundhiru man yakhshāhā: you are only a warner, and your warning benefits those who fear the Hour.

46.explain: When they see it, it will feel as if they had stayed, in the world or in their graves, only an ʿashiyyah, an afternoon, or its ḍuḥā, the morning.
